channel.title: MIA — Management Intelligence Alert
channel.description: daily selected and enriched macroeconomic and political news

item.title: The Iran conflict re-escalated hard — Hormuz re-closed, US strikes resumed, Iran's economy near collapse — and a Russian diesel-export ban put a fresh squeeze on fuel markets; on trade, Washington will not renew USMCA while Brussels and Beijing opened new fronts, and foreign carmakers kept losing China.
item.description:
• Iran war reignites and its economy cracks: Iran re-closed Hormuz and the US launched a third round of strikes, while Tehran privately warned it will run out of food and medicine by late August under the naval blockade.
  • Diesel is the new pressure point: Russia banned diesel exports, sending US diesel futures up 11% and European prices to a record — a more direct industrial-fuel shock than crude.
  • Trade fragmentation accelerates on every side: the US will not renew USMCA, the EU opened its first anti-dumping case against Chinese agriculture and cut steel quotas, and China banned helium exports.
  • Foreign carmakers keep losing China: German brands fell 30–41% and Japanese brands up to 35% in H1, even as China's exports topped one million cars in a single month.
  • Europe hardens its strategic autonomy: NATO signed USD 50bn in deals with Saab displacing Boeing, Germany funded 50,000 Ukrainian drones, and von der Leyen readied a supply-chain law.

item.title: The mid-June calm is gone: Iran re-closed the Strait of Hormuz after attacking a transiting ship, the US launched its third round of strikes since Tuesday, and Iran's own leadership privately admits the naval blockade has pushed the economy to collapse by late August.
item.description:
This overturns last week's "markets steady" picture. Overnight Saturday–Sunday, Iran announced a new Hormuz closure and struck a ship attempting to cross; the US retaliated with more than 100 strikes on military targets, and Iran fired drones and missiles at Gulf neighbours. Shipping has already thinned — only 14 commodity vessels transited on 8 July, versus a 34/day average after the June truce. The decisive new signal is internal: President Pezeshkian told the Supreme Leader the economy was "on the ropes" and offered to resign, and the central bank warned Iran cannot sell oil at needed volumes and will exhaust food and medical supplies by late August. That desperation is what could still force Tehran back to a deal, even as fighting resumes. India's small manufacturers are already bracing for higher input costs.

Industry Impact

For ACS this restores an active feedstock-risk regime after a fortnight of complacency. The key nuance is two-sided: escalation threatens naphtha, LPG and solvent supply through Hormuz, but Iran's economic desperation caps how long it can sustain a closure. Treat the next weeks as elevated-volatility rather than settled crisis, keep supply-contingency plans live, and watch the late-August Iranian deadline as the pivot between renewed talks and a deeper shock.

Les Echos | Fortune | Lianhe Zaobao | The Straits Times | LiveMint

item.title: Russia — the world's second-largest diesel exporter — banned diesel exports, driving US diesel futures up 11% and European prices to a record, while the IEA says global oil output is still 9.4 million bpd below pre-war levels and Eni warns crude could break USD 100 by early 2027.
item.description:
The new development is a shift in where the energy stress sits: from crude to refined product. Russia's diesel loadings collapsed to 234,000 bpd (1–10 July) from a 2025 average near 817,000, as Ukrainian strikes on refineries bite; the IEA cut Russia's 2026 output forecast to 8.9 million bpd. Diesel is the single largest share of global oil consumption — industrial machinery, farm equipment, heavy transport, power generation — so the ban ripples even to countries that do not buy Russian fuel. On crude, June output recovered to 98.8 mb/d but stayed ~9.4 mb/d below pre-war; the IMF pegs 2026 oil near USD 78. Eni's CEO warns finite stockpile releases have held prices in an USD 80–100 band that will break by Q1 2027 if the war continues, with every USD 5 rise adding ~USD 190bn to global costs.

Industry Impact

Diesel is the more direct hit to ACS economics than crude: it drives inbound raw-material freight, distribution and site logistics, so a sustained diesel premium raises landed input costs across the network regardless of feedstock prices. Combined with the renewed Hormuz risk (see other insight in this alert), the planning base should assume higher-for-longer energy and logistics costs through H2, with refined-product spikes the more probable channel than a crude blowout.

MarketScreener — diesel ban | The Economic Times | Le Figaro — IEA | MarketScreener — IEA Russia | Asharq Al-Awsat — Eni

item.title: The July WEO Update settled at 3.0% global growth for 2026 (3.4% in 2027), a rare China upgrade to 4.6%, and inflation raised to 4.7% — and the IMF now flags a second inflation driver alongside the war: an AI-investment frenzy.
item.description:
The full release confirms the two-speed picture but sharpens the inflation story. Growth is 3.0% (down 0.1), rising to 3.4% in 2027; the eurozone is stuck at 0.9% and the US resilient at 2.3% on AI investment. China is one of the few upgrades, +0.2 to 4.6%, on high-tech manufacturing and exports. Trade growth slows to 3.5% from 5%, and global energy prices sit ~25% above pre-conflict levels. The genuinely new emphasis: the IMF and central-bank commentary now name the AI-capex boom as a second inflation risk on top of the Middle East war — investment that lifts growth but also entrenches price stickiness. Country detail hardened around the conflict: Egypt was cut to 4.4% explicitly on Hormuz, while Thailand was nudged up to 1.9% on tech exports and stimulus.

Industry Impact

The demand map for ACS is unchanged but firmer: soft European volumes, strength concentrated in China, India and AI-linked electronics. The new inflation framing matters for margins — if AI capex keeps inflation sticky, rates stay higher for longer, raising financing costs for construction and capital-intensive customers even where output grows. Plan for demand strength and cost pressure to coexist, rather than expecting disinflation to relieve input costs.

China Economic Net | Kompas — two forces | The Economic Times — eurozone/US | Commercial Times — two inflation worries | Asharq Al-Awsat — Egypt | Bangkok Post — Thailand

item.title: Washington announced it will not renew the USMCA, moving North American trade to annual review and negotiation; at the same time a KPMG survey shows four in ten Canadian manufacturers have moved operations to the US or plan to, as tariffs reshape where factories sit.
item.description:
This is a genuinely new structural signal. USTR Jamieson Greer said the US will not renew the pact that replaced NAFTA in 2020, converting a stable framework into a year-by-year negotiation — a large source of uncertainty for the continent's integrated manufacturing base. The corporate response is already visible: KPMG finds 40% of Canadian manufacturers have relocated to the US or intend to, following Toyota's USD 3.6 billion San Antonio plant and its shift of Tacoma production out of Mexico over four years. A trade lawyer expects more such moves, with tariffs the decisive factor. One offsetting note of pragmatism: the US and Canada settled their Gordie Howe bridge dispute, which opens on 27 July.

Industry Impact

For ACS the read-through is a geographic redistribution of demand rather than a net loss: as automotive and industrial production migrates from Canada and Mexico into the US, adhesive, sealant and coating demand follows the plants. Suppliers with US manufacturing and logistics gain; those anchored to Canadian or Mexican production face customer relocation risk. The deeper problem is planning instability — an annually renegotiated USMCA makes multi-year North American footprint decisions harder to underwrite.

Food Tank | BNN Bloomberg | Der Standard — bridge deal

item.title: Trade defence is spreading into new sectors at once: the EU opened its first anti-dumping case against Chinese agriculture (Pekin ducks) and cut steel import quotas with a 50% above-quota tariff, while China retaliated in the strategic-materials domain with a ban on helium exports critical to chipmaking.
item.description:
The pattern this cycle is breadth. The EU launched an anti-dumping probe into Chinese duck meat — whole, cut and processed — after five producers alleged subsidies via China's five-year plans, singling out Shandong; it is the first extension of EU trade defence to Chinese agriculture, and lands the same week as definitive tyre duties of up to 45.3%. Separately, Brussels cut tariff-free steel imports 47% a day before July rules, exposing volumes to a 50% above-quota tariff, while UK importers got five days to absorb a 51% quota cut and an identical tariff. China's countermove targets the tech supply chain: a temporary export ban on helium, the irreplaceable "golden gas" used in wafer cooling, exposure and leak detection. Bayer also asked Washington for duties on Chinese glyphosate, and China set a 73.5% deposit on Canadian pea starch.

Industry Impact

Each front touches ACS differently but points the same way. Steel-quota tightening raises costs for metal-bonding and construction customers; agricultural anti-dumping signals that no sector is now off-limits, raising retaliation risk on EU chemical exports to China. The helium ban is the sharpest direct read: it threatens semiconductor output and, with it, demand for electronic adhesives, encapsulants and thermal materials (see other insight in this alert on Taiwan and chips). The strategic takeaway is to price trade policy as a permanent, multi-sector variable in sourcing and pricing.

South China Morning Post — ducks | Global Times — tyre duties | BSSA — steel quotas | Commercial Times — helium ban | Fortune — glyphosate

item.title: Ursula von der Leyen will propose a law to diversify strategically important supply chains, backed by a new G7 Critical Minerals Alliance, marking a shift to treating supply-chain resilience as economic and strategic security — with graphite named the first real test of the strategy.
item.description:
Alongside its trade-defence actions (see other insight in this alert), the EU is building an industrial-security architecture. The planned law responds to Chinese export restrictions on critical raw materials and reframes resilience as a security question, not just a commercial one. Graphite is the illustrative case: long treated as a minor battery input, it is now recognised as essential to advanced manufacturing, aerospace, defence systems, secure communications and energy storage — and heavily China-dependent. A parallel "solidarity instrument" would compensate firms that diversify supply chains away from China and cushion Chinese retaliation, though Chinese commentary derides it as the EU insuring against self-made risks, and it needs funding EU governments are struggling to agree. Separately, the EU Forced Labour Regulation ban takes effect 14 December 2027, adding a compliance layer across all supply-chain stages.

Industry Impact

For chemical and ACS producers this signals both opportunity and obligation. A designation-and-subsidy regime for strategic materials could support EU-based feedstock and specialty producers, while diversification incentives may de-risk raw-material sourcing over time. The Forced Labour Regulation, however, extends due-diligence exposure to every tier of the supply chain by end-2027 — a concrete compliance cost. Engage early on which materials and sites qualify as "critical," and begin mapping forced-labour exposure now.

Wallstreet-online | Initiative Mittelstand | China Daily — solidarity instrument | International Tin Association — forced-labour ban

item.title: Foreign carmakers are being pushed out of China simultaneously — German brands down 30–41% and Japanese brands up to 35% in H1 — while China's own exports topped one million vehicles in a single month for the first time, confirming a structural, not cyclical, shift.
item.description:
The scale is now unambiguous. H1 China passenger-car sales fell 24% to 8.3 million units; in Q2, VW's China deliveries dropped 37%, BMW/Mini 30%, Mercedes 28%, with the German majors down 30–41% overall. VW group sales fell 8.6%, the core brand 14%, prompting plans to halve its model lineup. The new element is confirmation that this is not only a German problem: Japanese H1 China sales fell across the board — Honda −34.7%, Toyota −17.1%, Nissan −15%. Meanwhile China's export engine hit a record: June car exports rose 75.1% to 1,037,800 units (NEVs +160%), H1 up 65.3% to 5.096 million, with AlixPartners projecting nearly 10 million for 2026. Europe carries ~3 million vehicles of overcapacity, half in Germany. Profit-per-vehicle fell for seven major global automakers in FY2025.

Industry Impact

This is the most important structural demand signal for European ACS. The German and Japanese automotive base — heavy consumers of structural adhesives, sealants and coatings — is losing its most profitable market permanently, so the legacy OEM adhesive pool will keep shrinking. Demand is relocating twice over: into Chinese OEMs (design-in and qualification are the offensive play) and into export markets receiving Chinese vehicles, including Europe. Reweight toward Chinese-OEM and aftermarket exposure, and treat European auto-adhesive volumes as a structurally declining base.

Fortune — H1 −24% | MarketScreener — German brands | Commercial Times — Japanese brands | Yahoo Taiwan — exports | Il Sole 24 Ore — overcapacity

item.title: NATO's Ankara summit produced USD 50 billion in new contracts — including Sweden's Saab displacing Boeing's AWACS fleet — while Germany funded 50,000 strike drones for Ukraine and US senators agreed a Russia secondary-sanctions bill, all pointing to a durable, Europe-weighted defence-demand pillar.
item.description:
The direction set at Ankara continues to firm. Beyond the headline USD 50 billion in deals, the symbolic shift is Saab replacing Boeing for airborne early warning — read explicitly as Europe and Canada moving toward security independence from Washington — alongside a NATO Defence Industrial Cooperation Strategy and a USD 40 billion+ anti-drone commitment. Germany's funding of 50,000 first-person-view strike drones (SkyFall airframes, US Auterion autonomous-targeting software) is one of the largest known Western drone orders and a marker of scaled, software-defined procurement. On the pressure side, four US senators agreed with the administration to advance a bill imposing secondary sanctions on buyers of Russian energy — a potential new lever over India and China. Iran, for its part, said it tripled drone production during the war, underscoring how drone manufacturing is now central to the conflict economy.

Industry Impact

Defence remains a growing, EUR-scale, Europe-weighted demand pillar for structural adhesives, composite bonding, sealants and specialty coatings across missiles, aircraft, drones and vehicles. The autonomy shift favours EU-based and ITAR-free suppliers, and the drone build-out adds a new high-volume, fast-cycle segment (lightweight bonding, potting, conformal coatings) distinct from long-cycle platforms. Position for both the long-programme and the emerging drone-manufacturing supply chains.

Bjd.com.cn — summit outcomes | La Vanguardia — USD 50bn / Saab | The Economic Times — German drones | MarketScreener — Russia sanctions bill | Anadolu Agency — Iran drones

item.title: Fed Chair Kevin Warsh named five task forces to overhaul the central bank's approach to communication, its balance sheet, data, employment and the inflation framework — just as the Fed's own report says inflation "stepped up further" in spring 2026, running near double the 2% target.
item.description:
This is a new, structural development in US monetary policy. Warsh appointed high-profile leads — including former RBI governor Raghuram Rajan, Harvard's Raj Chetty and Microsoft's Asha Sharma — to review whether the Fed's tools remain fit for an economy reshaped by AI, shifting labour supply and stickier inflation. The backdrop justifies the urgency: the first policy report under Warsh says core PCE is running around double the 2% objective as of May, even as the labour market has balanced at 4.2% unemployment, with labour-supply growth slowed by weaker immigration and ageing. The inflation signal is not only American — Japan's June PPI hit a three-year high of 7.1% on energy and AI-linked metals demand, German inflation held at 2.3%, UK GDP stagnated, and Canadian unemployment edged down to 6.5% even as manufacturing and construction shed ~30,000 jobs.

Industry Impact

A Fed rethinking its inflation framework amid above-target prices reinforces the higher-for-longer rate outlook that governs construction and capital-goods demand — the cyclical ACS end-markets most sensitive to financing costs. The global data spread (sticky Japanese and US inflation, flat UK, soft Canadian industry) argues against betting on a broad 2026 demand rebound in rate-sensitive segments. Plan for financing-cost headwinds to persist into 2027.

Hong Kong Commercial Daily — task forces | Business Standard — task-force leads | The Globe and Mail — inflation report | The Economic Times — Japan PPI | MarketScreener — Canada jobs

item.title: Taiwan's 2026 growth forecast was revised up to 9.64% — more than three times the global average — on an electronics and AI export surge, even as a McKinsey/SEMI study warns the US semiconductor industry faces a shortfall of 157,000 skilled workers by 2030, threatening flagship fabs.
item.description:
The AI-hardware cycle is producing extreme divergence. Taiwan's estimated 2026 GDP growth was lifted to 9.64% (Bloomberg estimates 9.5%), with listed-company earnings growth revised from ~20% to over 40% and electronics near 50%; semiconductors and tech hardware now make up 78% of the Taiwan exchange's value, up from 45% in 2015. Academia Sinica publishes its own revision on 13 July, against a December estimate of just 3.71% — the scale of upgrade is the story. But the constraint is talent: a McKinsey, SEMI and NSF study projects a US skilled-labour gap of 157,000 by 2030, worst in Texas, California, Arizona, New York and Ohio, jeopardising TSMC's up-to-USD 265 billion Arizona build, Micron's USD 100 billion New York plant and Samsung's Texas fab. India's IT minister puts the global gap near one million; Micron will invest over USD 250 billion by 2035.

Industry Impact

Electronics and semiconductors are where industrial ACS demand is growing fastest — die-attach adhesives, encapsulants, thermal-interface and conformal-coating materials scale directly with wafer and packaging output. Taiwan's boom is a demand tailwind; the US talent gap is a supply-timing risk that could delay the fab build-out and the associated materials ramp. China's helium ban (see other insight in this alert) is a further squeeze on the same chain. Align specialty-materials capacity with the AI-hardware cycle while watching for fab-schedule slippage.

Commercial Times — Taiwan 9.64% | Yahoo Taiwan — Bloomberg 9.5% | Cnyes — talent gap | The Economic Times — global gap | Cnyes — Micron

item.title: Typhoon Maysak triggered severe flooding across China's Guangxi region, while Typhoon Bavi — the largest to threaten northern Taiwan in about 25 years — cancelled more than 1,000 flights, closed Taipei and its stock market, and cut mountain roads, with peripheral effects reaching Liaoning and even a hurricane in Russia's Leningrad region.
item.description:
Extreme weather is again a live industrial-disruption factor. In Guangxi, Maysak — the year's tenth typhoon — flooded multiple areas; the Guigang Zoo was destroyed, with over 100 animals lost. China's telecoms sector alone dispatched emergency crews 68,000 times and restored 11,000 damaged base stations, indicating the breadth of infrastructure impact. In Taiwan, Bavi cancelled over 1,000 flights across 10–11 July and prompted Taipei to suspend work and classes, closing the stock exchange for a day; officials compared its potential impact to 2015's Typhoon Soudelor. Roads in Miaoli were severed, trapping residents. The system's periphery damaged farmland and roads in Liaoning, while a separate hurricane left 42,500 without power in Russia's Leningrad region.

Industry Impact

The direct exposure for ACS is through Taiwan and coastal China. Bavi's disruption threatens the island's electronics and semiconductor cluster — the same customers driving specialty-adhesive and encapsulant demand (see other insight in this alert) — through logistics and short production halts, while Guangxi flooding hits regional construction and distribution. The recurring pattern reinforces climate resilience as a demand driver over time (waterproofing membranes, sealants, protective coatings) even as it raises near-term supply-chain interruption risk in the Asian electronics base.

Xinhua — Guangxi | Global Times — Guigang Zoo | China Economic Net — telecoms response | Chinatimes — Taipei closure | Chinatimes — flights cancelled

item.title: China keeps pulling ahead in embodied AI — its G1 humanoid robot performed the world's first live surgery and installed industrial robots topped two million — while analysts warn the EU enters mass humanoid robotisation "from great weakness," having fallen from 26% to 17.6% of global GDP since 1993.
item.description:
The physical-AI theme sharpened this cycle. Unitree's G1 completed the first minimally invasive surgery by a humanoid robot (laparoscopic operations on live pigs), a capability milestone; China's installed industrial-robot base surpassed two million by 2024, and its AI industry exceeded CNY 1 trillion in 2025 with 30%+ growth forecast for 2026. Against this, a Thomas More Institute analysis warns the EU approaches humanoid robotisation from structural weakness — its share of global GDP fell from 25.99% to 17.57% since 1993, France's by 43.7%. The counter-current is caution: a McKinsey survey finds only 27% of leaders think their organisations are ready for agentic AI, and markets had a volatile week on renewed "AI bubble" worries — a reminder the build-out is real but the valuations are contested.

Industry Impact

Robotics and embodied AI are an expanding, adhesive-, encapsulant- and thermal-material-intensive demand pool, and China's lead means the fastest-growing volumes sit in Asia. The European competitiveness warning is the demand risk: if EU industrial output continues to erode, so does its ACS consumption base. Position materials capacity toward Asian and US robotics and AI-hardware chains, while monitoring European industrial policy (see other insight in this alert on the supply-chain law) as the potential offset.

Les Echos — EU weakness | Commercial Times — G1 surgery | South China Morning Post — 2m robots | Commercial Times — growth engine | The Economic Times — McKinsey readiness

item.title: Peru elected pro-US Keiko Fujimori by a razor-thin ~0.27 points, keeping the China-invested Chancay Port a US–China flashpoint, while Colombia's power transfer stalled as outgoing President Petro alleged fraud — prompting the US and regional allies to demand an orderly handover by 6 August.
item.description:
Two Latin American results carry direction-setting weight. In Peru, Fujimori won by around 40,000 votes on a "dual insurance" posture — pro-US politically while economically reliant on China — with attention on the Chinese-built Chancay Port (2025: USD 603 million of exports, 336,200 TEU throughput), located 60km from a port near a US naval base. In Colombia, president-elect Abelardo de la Espriella suspended the formal transition after the Petro government questioned the result; the US, Argentina, Ecuador, El Salvador and other Trump-aligned states urged Bogotá to respect the constitution, with Petro now saying he will hand over on 6 August while still disputing the outcome. In Europe, Germany's Merz is running a "Reformkanzler" campaign ahead of 20 September state elections in Berlin and Saxony-Anhalt, where the AfD leads polls.

Industry Impact

The direct ACS exposure is limited, but both results shape trade and investment geography. Peru's tilt keeps Chancay — a growing Pacific gateway for South American trade — in play amid US–China rivalry, relevant to regional logistics and materials flows. Colombia's contested transition adds Andean political risk. The more material watch item for European demand is Germany's autumn state elections, where an AfD advance would raise policy uncertainty for the country's industrial and fiscal direction.

Chinatimes — Peru | Süddeutsche Zeitung — Colombia | Politico — Merz | Süddeutsche Zeitung — Berlin CDU

item.title: Five developing storylines with known dates: Academia Sinica's Taiwan forecast, the India–UK FTA, the Iranian late-August supply deadline, the Gordie Howe bridge opening, and Germany's September state elections.
item.description:
• 13 July — Academia Sinica revises Taiwan's 2026 forecast: the scale of upgrade from December's 3.71% will confirm how far the AI-hardware boom has reshaped the outlook that drives electronics-materials demand.
  • 15 July — India–UK FTA enters into force: car import duty falls from 110% to 30% on a 20,000-unit quota; a first read on specialty-goods and automotive market access, though gains depend on certification and logistics.
  • Late August — Iran's food and medical supply deadline: Tehran's own warning of when the naval blockade becomes untenable — the pivot between renewed talks and a deeper energy shock.
  • 27 July — Gordie Howe Detroit–Windsor bridge opens: a rare point of US–Canada de-escalation against the USMCA-renewal uncertainty reshaping North American manufacturing.
  • 20 September — Berlin and Saxony-Anhalt state elections: a strong AfD showing would raise policy uncertainty for Germany's industrial and fiscal direction and, with it, the swing factor for European demand.
